To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
visual feedback is important to all ages, but is especially important to children.
visual feedback is preferred and is used to help users make more interpretable gestures.
visual feedback improves the accuracy and efficiency of surface gesture recognition, and children prefer to see visual traces of their gestures.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of visual feedback on surface gesture interaction and the design of gesture interfaces on mobile touchscreen devices, and provides insights for the design of gesture-based mobile applications.
how children, teens, adults, and designers can benefit from visual feedback for surface gesture interfaces on mobile touchscreen devices.
the usability of visual surface gestures on mobile touchscreen devices and how it is affected by the age of the user.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children, teens, or adults prefer to see the visual feedback when they are doing gestures on the mobile touchscreen device.
visual feedback improves the quality of surface gestures and is beneficial to children, teens, adults and all users.
children are not as accurate as adults, and they need to be able to see the gesture they are making in order to be accurate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
children and teens are more consistent and more likely to make the same gestures as adults when visual feedback is provided.
children are more likely to make gestures with more strokes, and more likely to make shorter, less compact strokes when visual feedback is not available.
the more complex the gesture, the more likely it is to be affected by the presence or absence of visual feedback.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the absence of visual trace can lead to a significant change in how gestures are performed.
visual feedback can be beneficial for all users, but especially for children.
users of all ages tend to interact differently with and without visual traces of their gestures.
